'''Neil Adam Gershenfeld''' (born December 1, 1959) is an American physicist. He is a professor in the [[MIT]] Program in Media Arts and Sciences<ref name="e310">{{cite web | title=Massachusetts Institute of Technology | website=MIT | url=https://web.mit.edu/directory/?id=gersh&d=cba.mit.edu }}</ref> and the director of the MIT [[Center for Bits and Atoms]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Neil Gershenfeld biography |url=http://ng.cba.mit.edu/neil/bio.html |website=ng.cba.mit.edu |access-date=April 26, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120712151444/http://ng.cba.mit.edu/neil/bio.html |archive-date=July 12, 2012 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> He works mainly on [[interdisciplinary]] topics in [[physics]] and [[computer science]], such as [[quantum computing]], [[nanotechnology]], and personal [[Digital fabricator|fabrication]]. He has been called the "intellectual father of the [[maker movement]]".<ref>{{cite web |title=Making (Almost) Anything |work=Spectrum |date=Fall 2019 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://betterworld.mit.edu/spectrum/issues/fall-2019/making-almost-anything/ }}</ref> 

==Early life and education==
Gershenfeld was born on December 1, 1959 in [[Ardmore, Pennsylvania]] to a Jewish family.<ref name="w071">{{cite book | last=National Academy of Arbitrators Annual Meeting | title=Arbitration 2010 | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-61746-000-5 | page=xxii | url=https://naarb.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/2010-0.pdf}}</ref><ref name="z564">{{cite web | last=Funeral | first=Goldsteins | title=Walter Gershenfeld Obituary | website=Goldsteins Funeral | date=2022-05-05 | url=https://obits.goldsteinsfuneral.com/walter-gershenfeld-1 }}</ref> His father, Walter Gershenfeld, was a labor arbitrator and mediator and emeritus professor of management at Temple University,<ref name="l101">{{cite web | last=Downey | first=Sally A. | title=Walter J. Gershenfeld, 84, management professor | website=Inquirer.com | date=2010-02-27 | url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/obituaries/20100227_Walter_J__Gershenfeld__84__management_professor.html }}</ref> and his mother Gladys Gershenfeld who was also an arbitrator.<ref name="o527">{{cite web | last=Saulnier | first=Beth | title=The Replicator Revolution – Cornell Alumni Magazine | website=Cornell Alumni Magazine – Your alma mater, your stories, your magazine | date=2021-10-16 | url=https://cornellalumnimagazine.com/the-replicator-revolution/ }}</ref><ref name="a193">{{cite web | title=Guide to the Gershenfeld, Walter and Gladys Arbitration Papers, 1932-2010 | website=Rare and Manuscript Collections | url=https://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/KCL06344.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130607034913/http://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/KCL06344.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=June 7, 2013 }}</ref> 

He attended [[Plymouth-Whitemarsh High School]] in [[Plymouth Meeting, Pennsylvania]]. Later he attended [[Swarthmore College]], graduating in 1981 with a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] degree in [[physics]] with high honors.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ng.cba.mit.edu/neil/cv.pdf |title=CV: Prof. Neil Gershenfeld |website=ng.cba.mit.edu |access-date=July 30, 2015}}</ref> In 1990, he earned a [[Doctor of Science|Ph.D.]] in [[physics]] at [[Cornell University]]; his thesis was titled ''Representation of chaos''.<ref>{{cite thesis |type=Ph.D. |publisher=[[Cornell University]] |publication-place= |last=Gershenfeld |first=Neil |date=1990 |title=Representation of chaos |oclc=64017404 |hdl= |doi= |osti= |url=https://catalog.library.cornell.edu/catalog/1745970 }}</ref>

He received an honorary doctorate from Swarthmore College in 2006.<ref>{{cite web |last=Gershenfeld |first=Neil |title=Swarthmore Commencement Address -- Neil Gershenfeld '81  |work=[[Swarthmore College]] |date=May 2006 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://www.swarthmore.edu/past-commencements/swarthmore-commencement-address-neil-gershenfeld-81 }}</ref>  In 2012 he received an honorary doctorate from [[Strathclyde University]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Oscar Pistorius to be awarded honorary degree from Strathclyde |work=Strathclyde Telegraph |date=October 11, 2012 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://strathclydetelegraph.com/2012/10/11/oscar-pistorius-to-be-awarded-honorary-degree-from-strathclyde/ }}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:Neil-gershenfeld-by-bill-cramer.jpg|thumb|Gershenfeld in 2008]]
[[File:Neil Gershenfeld APMM 2010.jpg|thumb|Gershenfeld as keynote speaker at APMM 2010]]
In 1998, Gershenfeld started a class at MIT called "How to make (almost) anything". Gershenfeld wanted to introduce expensive, industrial-size machines to the technical students. However, this class attracted a lot of students from various backgrounds: artists, architects, designers, students without any technical background. In his interview to [[CNN]], Gershenfeld said that "the students... were answering a question I didn't ask, which is: What is this stuff good for? And the answer is: Not to make what you can buy in stores, but to make what you can't buy in stores. It's to personalise fabrication".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://edition.cnn.com/videos/bestoftv/2013/07/17/exp-gps-gershenfeld-3d-printing.cnn |title=On GPS: Future of digital fabrication |last=Zakaria |first=Fareed |publisher=CNN website |date=July 17, 2013 |access-date=July 21, 2014}}</ref> Gershenfeld believes that this is the beginning of a new revolution: digital revolution in fabrication that will allow people to fabricate things, machines on demand.

Gershenfeld has presented his course on "How to make (almost) anything" at the Association of Professional Model Makers (APMM) 2010 Conference.<ref>{{cite web |title=APMM 2010 Conference – Keynote Professor Neil Gershenfeld |url=http://www.prototypetoday.com/apmm/apmm-2010-conference-keynote-professor-neil-gershenfeld |publisher=Prototype Today |date=2010 |access-date=April 21, 2014}}</ref>  In 2023, his course won the Irwin Sizer Award for the Most Significant Improvement to MIT education.<ref>{{cite web |title=Irwin Sizer Award: 2023 |work=MIT Awards Convocation |date=2023 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://ng.cba.mit.edu/show/slide/24.06.HTMAASizer.html }}</ref>  

This class later has led Gershenfeld to create [[Fab lab]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200604/gershenfeld.cfm |title=Gershenfeld Hopes to Spearhead a Fab-ulous Revolution |last=Tretkoff |first=Ernie |publisher=American Physical Society |date=April 6, 2006 |access-date=April 18, 2014}}</ref>  Gershenfeld feels very passionate about this project, as he believes that teaching kids how to use technology and create it themselves will empower the future generations to become more independent and create technology that each individual community needs, not a technology that is currently available on the market. Fab labs exist in over 150 countries.<ref>{{cite web |last= |first= |title=LabsMap |work=FabLabs |date= |access-date=2024-04-01 |url=https://fablabs.io/labs/map }}</ref>  In his interview with [[Discover (magazine)|''Discover'' magazine]] on the question what personal fabrication might be useful for, Gershenfeld said, "There is a surprising need for emergent technologies in many of the least developed places on the planet. While our needs might be fairly well met, there are billions of people on the planet whose needs are not. Their problems don't need incremental tweaks in current technology, but a revolution".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Svitil |first=Kathy A. |date=January 1, 2003 |title=Physicist Neil Gershenfeld—Time to Make the Computer Vanish |url=http://discovermagazine.com/2003/jan/breakdialogue#.UdUBOTvFVqw |journal=[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]] |publisher=[[Kalmbach Publishing]] |volume=26 |issue=1 |access-date=July 22, 2014}}</ref>

Gershenfeld chairs Fab Foundation,<ref>{{cite web |title=Fab Foundation Board |work=Fab Foundation |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://fabfoundation.org/about/#board-team }}</ref> leads the Fab Academy,<ref>{{cite web |title=Meet Our People: Program Director |work=Fab Academy |quote=Neil leads the academy |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://fabacademy.org/about/people.html }}</ref> which grew into the "Academany" platform for distributed hands-on education.<ref>{{cite web |title=About |work=Academany |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://academany.org/about/ }}</ref> 

In addition to the "How to make (almost) anything" course, Gershenfeld has taught "How To Make Something That Makes (almost) Anything", "The Physics of Information Technology", "The Nature of Mathematical Modeling".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ng.cba.mit.edu/neil/classes.html |title=List of Neil Gershenfeld classes |website=ng.cba.mit.edu |last=Gershenfeld |first=Neil |access-date=April 26, 2014}}</ref>

He was involved in starting the [[Interspecies Internet]] where he is a Founding Trustee.<ref name="TED2013">{{cite web | title=The interspecies internet? An idea in progress |work=Ted Talks |date=February 2013 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/diana_reiss_peter_gabriel_neil_gershenfeld_and_vint_cerf_the_interspecies_internet_an_idea_in_progress }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Team |work=Interspecies Internet |quote=Founding Trustee |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://www.interspecies.io/team }}</ref> 

Gershenfeld has spoken at [[TED (conference)|TED conferences]],<ref name="TED2013" /> and presented at the World Economic Forum in Davos.<ref>{{cite web |title=Progressive Companies Make Leap from Sustainable to “Circular” Manufacturing |date=January 25, 2014 |work=World Economic Forum |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://www.weforum.org/press/2014/01/progressive-companies-make-leap-from-sustainable-to-circular-manufacturing/ }}</ref>

===Quantum computing pioneer===
In 1998, Gershenfield and associates built the first quantum computer (2-qubit) that could be loaded with data and output a solution. Although impractical, it demonstrated the principles of quantum computation, it was the first significant faster-than-classical quantum computation.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Experimental Implementation of Fast Quantum Searching |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=80 |issue=15 |pages=3408–3411 |publisher=The American Physical Society |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.3408 |year=1998 |last1=Chuang |first1=Isaac L. |author-link=Isaac Chuang |last2=Gershenfeld |first2=Neil |last3=Kubinec |first3=Mark |bibcode=1998PhRvL..80.3408C }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Holton |first=William Coffeen |title=quantum computer |url=https://www.britannica.com/technology/quantum-computer |access-date=4 Dec 2021 |newspaper=Encyclopedia Britannica |publisher=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]}}</ref> 

===Ultralight material===
In 2013, Gershenfeld and fellow researchers at MIT introduced [[reversibly assembled cellular composite materials]].<ref name=sci>{{Cite journal | last1 = Cheung | first1 = K. C. | last2 = Gershenfeld | first2 = N. | title = Reversibly Assembled Cellular Composite Materials | doi = 10.1126/science.1240889 | journal = Science | year = 2013 | pmid =  23950496| volume=341 | issue = 6151 | pages=1219–1221| bibcode = 2013Sci...341.1219C | citeseerx = 10.1.1.672.1351 | s2cid = 206550070 }}</ref><ref name=kurz>{{cite journal|url=http://www.kurzweilai.net/assembling-big-structures-out-of-small-ultralight-pieces |title=Assembling big structures out of small ultralight pieces |journal=Science |volume=341 |issue=6151 |pages=1219–1221 |doi=10.1126/science.1240889 |pmid=23950496 |date=2013-07-17 |access-date=2013-08-20|last1=Cheung |first1=K. C. |last2=Gershenfeld |first2=N. |citeseerx=10.1.1.672.1351 |s2cid=206550070 }}</ref>

===Other research ===
[[File:Neil Gershenfeld TAM 5.jpg|thumb|Gershenfeld with [[James Randi]] at [[The Amaz!ng Meeting|TAM 5]]]]
His work has been published in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', ''Nature'', IEEE, ACM, ''Cell'', and many other journals, as well as in The [[American Physical Society]] journal. 

Gershenfeld published an early paper on what became known as the [[Internet of Things]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gershenfeld |first1=Neil |last2=Krikorian |first2=Raffi |last3=Cohen |first3=Danny |title=The internet of things |journal=Scientific American |date=2004 |volume=291 |number=4 |pages=76-81}}</ref> His paper "Microfluidic bubble logic" introduced digital logic in [[microfluidics]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Microfluidic Bubble Logic |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1136907 |journal=Science |access-date=April 26, 2014 |last1=Gershenfeld |first1=Neil |last2=Prakash |first2=Manu |date=February 9, 2007|volume=315 |issue=5813 |pages=832–5 |doi=10.1126/science.1136907 |pmid=17289994 |bibcode=2007Sci...315..832P |s2cid=5882836 |hdl=1721.1/46593 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> His paper on "Physical one-way functions" introduced the concept of [[Types of physical unclonable function|physical one-way functions]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Physical one-way functions |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1074376 |journal=Science |access-date=April 26, 2014 |last1=Gershenfeld |first1=Neil |last2=Pappu |first2=Ravikanth |last3=Recht |first3=Ben |last4=Taylor |first4=Jason |date=September 20, 2002|volume=297 |issue=5589 |pages=2026–30 |doi=10.1126/science.1074376 |pmid=12242435 |bibcode=2002Sci...297.2026P |hdl=1721.1/45499 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

Gershenfeld released the ''Great Invention Kit'' in 2008, a construction set that users can manipulate to create various objects.<ref>{{cite web |last=Greenberg |first=Andy |title=Invention kits let you build (almost) anything |date=August 21, 2008 |url=http://www.nbcnews.com/id/26319233/ns/technology_and_science-tech_and_gadgets/t/invention-kits-let-you-build-almost-anything/#.UdT9ojvFVqw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202210454/http://www.nbcnews.com/id/26319233/ns/technology_and_science-tech_and_gadgets/t/invention-kits-let-you-build-almost-anything/#.UdT9ojvFVqw |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 2, 2013 |publisher=NBC News |access-date=July 4, 2013}}</ref>

==Honors and recognition==
Gershenfeld is a [[List of fellows of the American Physical Society (1998–2010)|Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (2007).<ref>{{cite web |title=Awards and honors |work=MIT News |date=December 12, 2007 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2007/aandh-tt1212 }}</ref>  He is a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science|Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2020).<ref>{{cite web |title=Six MIT faculty elected 2020 AAAS Fellows |work=MIT News |date=November 24, 2020 |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2020/six-faculty-2020-aaas-fellows-1124 }}</ref> He is an elected [[List of members of the National Academy of Engineering (computer science)|Member of the National Academy of Engineering]] (2023).<ref>{{cite web |title=Members: Dr. Neil Gershenfeld |work=[[National Academy of Engineering]] |access-date=2026-03-30 |url=https://www.nae.edu/19579/19581/20412/290212/Dr-Neil-Gershenfeld }}</ref> 

''[[Scientific American]]'' named Gershenfeld one of their "[[Scientific American 50]]" for 2004 and has also named him Communications Research Leader of the Year.<ref name="SciAm2004">{{cite news |pages=47 |title=The Scientific American 50 |date=December 2004 |publisher=Scientific American |url=http://www.sciam.com/article.cfm?articleID=000D5CA6-D59B-118F-91DD83414B7F0000&pageNumber=2&catID=9}}</ref> Gershenfeld has been featured in ''[[The New York Times]]'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/05/15/magazine/the-kitchen-table-industrialists.html?pagewanted=2 |title=The Kitchen-Table Industrialists |last=Giridharadas |first=Anand |newspaper=The New York Times |date=May 13, 2011 |access-date=April 4, 2014}}</ref> in ''[[The Economist]]'',<ref name="The Economist">{{cite web |title=How to make (almost) anything |url=https://www.economist.com/technology-quarterly/2005/06/11/how-to-make-almost-anything |magazine=The Economist |access-date=April 4, 2014 |author=the printed edition |date=June 9, 2005}}</ref> and on [[NPR]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Making of a Personal Lab |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=5008294 |publisher=[[NPR]] |access-date=April 4, 2014 |date=November 11, 2005}}</ref>
He was named as one of the 40 modern-day Leonardos by the [[Museum of Science and Industry (Chicago)|Museum of Science and Industry Chicago]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Modern-Day Leonardos |url=http://www.msichicago.org/scrapbook/scrapbook_exhibits/leonardo/modern/bios2/gershenfeld.html |publisher=Museum of Science and Industry Chicago |access-date=April 18, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140727013016/http://www.msichicago.org/scrapbook/scrapbook_exhibits/leonardo/modern/bios2/gershenfeld.html |archive-date=July 27, 2014 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> ''[[Prospect (magazine)|Prospect]]'' named him as one of the top 100 public intellectuals.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.prospectmagazine.co.uk/magazine/100-top-public-intellectuals |title=Intellectuals—the results |publisher=Prospect |date=July 26, 2008 |access-date=July 21, 2014}}</ref>

== Jeffrey Epstein encounters ==
In July 2019, it was revealed that the director of the MIT Media Lab, [[Joi Ito]], had accepted several large donations from [[Jeffrey Epstein]]; Ito later resigned in the ensuing scandal.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/07/business/mit-media-lab-jeffrey-epstein-joichi-ito.html|work=The New York Times|title=Director of M.I.T.'s Media Lab Resigns After Taking Money From Jeffrey Epstein|last1=Tracy|first1=Marc|last2=Hsu|first2=Tiffany|date=7 September 2019 |access-date=2020-01-27}}</ref> According to a 2020 investigation by [[Goodwin Procter]], published at the request of the MIT Corporation, Gershenfeld and other faculty had encountered Epstein three times during MIT Lab tours between June and October 2013. During one tour, Esptein expressed an interest in Gershenfeld's research work including consciousness, and signaling and deception by animals.<ref name="o879" /> After the initial meeting at MIT, Gershenfeld accepted a dinner invitation to Epstein's home in New York City.<ref name="o879">{{cite web | title=Report concerning Jeffrey Epstein's interactions with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology | url=https://facultygovernance.mit.edu/sites/default/files/20200121GoodwinProcterReport.pdf | date=2020-01-10 | access-date=July 22, 2025 }}</ref> Confirming this, emails from the Epstein files showed that in 2013, Epstein requested that Gershenfeld invite artist [[Jeff Koons]] to Epstein's home for dinner.<ref name="f368">{{cite web | title=Jeff Koons Attended Dinner Party at Jeffrey Epstein's House | website=Hyperallergic | date=2026-02-02 | url=https://hyperallergic.com/jeff-koons-attended-dinner-party-at-jeffrey-epsteins-house/ }}</ref><ref name="v217">{{cite web | last=Greenberger | first=Alex | title=Jeff Koons Says He 'Did Not Have a Relationship' with Jeffrey Epstein After Appearing in Files | website=ARTnews.com | date=2026-02-03 | url=https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/jeff-koons-jeffrey-epstein-statement-studio-visit-1234771956/ }}</ref>
